title: Bless, O my soul (Berakhot 10a)
hook: David says "Bless the LORD, O my soul" five times, for five stages of life
tomorrow: what did the sages pray when nobody handed them the words?

segments.voice: That was a week of hands and mercy: give me your hand, God carries us, mercy over anger, bless the one above, four cubits, and yesterday, don't despair of mercy, even with a sword on your neck.
screen: `A WEEK OF HANDS AND MERCY.` → `DON'T DESPAIR OF MERCY.`

segments.voice: Some songs repeat one line so many times it should get old, and somehow it lands harder every time. King David has a line like that: Bless the LORD, O my soul. Across the Psalms he says it five times. Right after Hezekiah's story, Berakhot asks the obvious question. Why five?
screen: `ONE LINE, OVER AND OVER.` → `BLESS THE LORD, O MY SOUL.` → `WHY FIVE TIMES?`

segments.voice: One answer comes in Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi's name: David said it once for each of the five worlds he lived in. In his mother's womb. When he came out into the world and looked up at the stars. When he nursed at his mother's breast. When he saw the wicked fall. And when he looked toward the day of his death. Five stages of a life, and the same line at every one. The psalm opens: "Bless the LORD, O my soul; and all that is within me, bless His holy name." Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in this reading, David blesses God before he was even born, and again facing his own death. The line doesn't wait for the good chapter. It goes with him through all of them. That's the word: bless. Not a feeling you wait for, but a line you bring into each stage, the hard ones from this week too: a sickbed, a small apartment, a sword on the neck.
screen: `FIVE TIMES, FIVE WORLDS.` · `THE WOMB, THE STARS, THE BREAST.` · `THE WICKED FALL, THE LAST DAY.` · `IT DOESN'T WAIT FOR THE GOOD PART.` · then, large: `BLESS, O MY SOUL.`

segments.voice: Count back through the stages of your life so far on your fingers: small child, school, now, and whatever came between. Stop on one stage, maybe a hard one, and find one thing in it you're grateful for. If you pray, you can say David's line over it; if not, simply hold it with thanks for the rest of the sit.
screen: `COUNT THE STAGES.` · `STOP ON ONE.` · `ONE THING TO THANK.`

segments.voice: Bless. David's five-times line, Bless the LORD, O my soul, said at every stage of a life.
Your line: bless, O my soul, in every stage, the hard ones too. Eleven days into Berakhot, and counting.

screen: `DAY 1498 COUNTS.` → `BERAKHOT · 11 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DID THE SAGES PRAY WHEN NOBODY HANDED THEM THE WORDS?`

howItsDone: Psalm 104, which opens 'Bless the LORD, O my soul', is said in many communities on Rosh Chodesh, the start of a new month, and some say it on Shabbat afternoons in the winter.

match.prompt: five worlds, one line — tap the pairs.

myth: David says 'Bless the LORD, O my soul' just once, at the start of a psalm
Berakhot counts five times across the Psalms, and asks why.
in one reading, David blesses God even in his mother's womb
the first of five worlds, in Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi's name.
all five stages are happy ones
they include seeing the wicked fall and looking toward the day of death.

fork.setup: your aunt says she'll start counting her blessings once this rough year is over. what does Berakhot 10a suggest?
options: David blessed at every stage, hard ones too; it doesn't wait for the good chapter.
wait; a blessing only means something when life is going well.
bless only the past; the present is too close to see clearly yet.
fork.reveal: five stages, from before birth to the day of death, and the same line at each one. the blessing goes with David through all of them.

original.note: Hebrew: bless, O my soul, the opening of Psalms 103 and 104.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty line repeated for the sound of it.
what it means: five times, for five stages of a life, from the womb to the day of death.
what a scholar hears: Psalms 103 and 104 hold the five; Berakhot 10a gives more than one reading, the five worlds in Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi's name and a parallel between the soul and God.
guess: to praise and thank God with your whole self
to ask God to keep you safe from all harm
to sprinkle water on someone as a sign of welcome
recall: the bond goes both ways: God carries us
may My mercy overcome My anger
even at the edge, keep asking

chat.says: first shabbat in saba's new place. he made kiddush, then looked at me and got teary. why?
options: Maybe it's David's line: bless, O my soul, at every stage. Even a new one.
He's sad the old house is gone; Shabbat there was the real one.
Kiddush is meant to make people cry; that's part of the blessing.
chat.meaning: In Berakhot 10a David blesses at each of five stages of life, even the last. A new stage, in a small apartment, still gets the line.

Psalms.meaning: the Bible's book of songs and prayers, many linked to David

Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi.meaning: a sage of the Talmud in the land of Israel

Hezekiah.meaning: a king of Judah who prayed when told he would die

Berakhot.meaning: blessings; the Talmud's tractate on the Shema, prayer and blessings

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 10a (five times 'Bless the LORD, O my soul'; Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi: five worlds David lived in)
